shared.title: The Monarch Butterfly Migration
shared.text:
Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies in eastern North America begin one of the most remarkable journeys in the insect world. They fly south thousands of kilometers to spend the winter in a small number of mountain forests in central Mexico. There, they gather in dense clusters on fir trees, where the cool but rarely freezing temperatures allow them to conserve energy until spring.

What makes this migration especially puzzling is that no single butterfly completes the entire round trip. The monarchs that fly south in the fall belong to a special generation that can live for about eight months, far longer than the few weeks typical of summer monarchs. In spring, these long-lived butterflies travel north and lay eggs on milkweed, the only plant their caterpillars can eat. Their offspring continue the journey, and it takes several generations to reach the northern breeding grounds again. Yet the next autumn, butterflies that have never made the trip find their way back to the same forests.

Scientists have discovered that monarchs navigate partly by using the position of the sun, adjusting for its movement across the sky with an internal clock in their antennae. However, the migration now faces threats. The loss of milkweed on farmland and the clearing of the Mexican forests have reduced the number of overwintering monarchs, leading conservation groups to plant milkweed along the migration route.

shared.title: How the Impressionists broke with tradition
shared.text:
Okay, so today we're going to look at how the Impressionists broke away from the art establishment in nineteenth-century France. To understand that, you need to know what they were rebelling against. At the time, the French Academy of Fine Arts more or less controlled what counted as good art. Every year there was an official exhibition called the Salon, and if your painting wasn't accepted there, it was really hard to build a career.

The Academy had pretty clear rules. The most respected paintings showed scenes from history, mythology, or the Bible. They were usually painted in a studio, with smooth surfaces where you couldn't see the brushstrokes, and with very careful, detailed finishing.

Now, the Impressionists, painters like Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, did pretty much the opposite. First, they chose everyday subjects: people relaxing in parks, train stations, boats on a river. Second, they often painted outdoors, which was made a lot easier by a fairly new invention, paint sold in portable metal tubes. And third, they used quick, visible brushstrokes to capture the changing effects of light. To many critics, their pictures looked unfinished, like sketches.

Not surprisingly, a lot of these works were rejected by the Salon. So in 1874, the group did something bold. They organized their own independent exhibition. A critic who reviewed it made fun of Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, and he used the word "Impressionists" as an insult. The artists, well, they ended up adopting the name.

So the real break wasn't just about style. It was also about showing that artists could find an audience without the Academy's approval.
